articles.title: As public trust declines, Muslim politicians are rising to the occasion
articles.summary: Declining trust in institutions widens what political scientists call the representation gap.
articles.body:
Zohran Mamdani’s historic victory was not only a milestone for Muslim Americans. It was also a window into a moment when voters increasingly turned to outsiders as their confidence in established institutions declined.

The easy explanation for the wave of Muslim American political success — Mamdani in New York, Reps. Ilhan Omar (D-Minn.) and Rashida Tlaib (D-Mich.) in the House, Abdul El-Sayed running for the Senate in Michigan — is that the country has simply grown more tolerant. That’s part of it.

But tolerance alone can’t explain why these particular candidates are winning, or why it’s happening at a moment when Americans of every background have grown skeptical of those who claim to represent them.

Start with trust. In 1958, 73 percent of Americans told pollsters they trusted the federal government to do the right thing most of the time. Today that figure sits at 17 percent , according to Pew Research Center — near the lowest point ever recorded. Layer on economic strain: A record 55 percent of Americans say their financial situation is getting worse, the fifth straight year that trend has held, per Gallup.

People who believe their government doesn’t work for them, and whose finances keep deteriorating anyway, are people primed to look past the usual political class for someone new. This is where the real mechanism lives, and it’s more precise than the idea that Americans vote for Muslim candidates because they distrust the government.

What happens instead is a chain. Declining trust in institutions widens what political scientists call the representation gap — the sense that officials, whatever their party, have drifted from the people who elected them. That gap makes voters more open to candidates who can credibly claim distance from the establishment, whether the outsider is Muslim, an immigrant, or neither.

Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.) and Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (D-N.Y.) rode the same opening, and neither fits the demographic profile of a beneficiary of rising tolerance. What connected them to Mamdani wasn’t identity. It was position — all three ran as alternatives to a political class voters had already stopped believing in.

The same distrust that creates opportunities for marginalized candidates can also empower demagogues; outsider status is a political opening, not a guarantee of democratic renewal. Distrust creates the opening. It doesn’t decide who walks through it. That’s the part of the story that belongs to Muslim Americans specifically, and it has almost nothing to do with luck.

For two decades, Muslim American civic organizations — the Council on American-Islamic Relations, Engage Action and others — built the unglamorous infrastructure of political power: voter registration drives, candidate training, donor networks, relationships with local party officials.

It shows up in the numbers. Voter registration among eligible Muslim Americans rose from 60 percent in 2016 to 85 percent in 2025 , according to the Institute for Social Policy and Understanding. It’s a jump that didn’t happen by accident, in a community that is also now the youngest religious group in the country.

Muslim Americans did not simply benefit when the political door swung open to outsiders. They spent a decade building the institutions capable of walking through it the moment it did.

That combination — a wide-open opportunity structure plus a community that had already done the organizing work to exploit it — is a better explanation for this moment than either factor alone. Distrust without organizing capacity produces protest votes and one-off insurgent candidacies that rarely last. Organizing capacity without a receptive political climate produces well-run campaigns that lose. Muslim American political success in 2025 and 2026 sits at the intersection of both.

But there’s a limit to what any of this proves, and it’s worth being honest about it. Winning office is a measure of political belonging — whether institutions include you. It is not the same as social belonging — whether the broader society has accepted you as an unremarkable, fully legitimate part of the national fabric. Those two things move at different speeds, through different mechanisms, and one doesn’t guarantee the other.

The same year Muslim American voter registration hit a record high, 63 percent of American Muslims reported experiencing religious discrimination in the past 12 months, the highest rate of any faith group surveyed by Institute for Social Policy and Understanding. A historic election is real evidence of institutional change. It is not proof that the underlying social climate has shifted to match it, and treating one as confirmation of the other is a mistake worth resisting; however good the headlines feel.

That distinction points to the larger question this moment actually raises, and it’s bigger than any single community. American democracy is not only being tested on whether it can let new groups into the rooms where power is exercised — it has been doing that, unevenly but persistently, for generations. It is being tested on something harder: whether its institutions can rebuild a working relationship with citizens across every background, who have concluded in remarkably consistent numbers that nobody in government is listening to them.

Electing outsiders is not a substitute for that repair. At best, it is evidence that voters are still willing to take a chance that someone might.

Wahid Gulrani, Ph.D. is a political sociologist and scholar of Afghanistan whose work focuses on security, migration and irregular warfare.

articles.body:
CNN political commentator Bakari Sellers on Friday said President Trump is being “bullied” by Canada amid an escalating trade war, comparing the current president’s handling of Canada with that of previous administrations.

“We’re getting bullied by Canada,” he said during a CNN panel discussion. “Joe Biden didn’t get bullied by Canada. Barack Obama didn’t get bullied by Canada. George W. Bush didn’t get bullied by Canada.”

Sellers also slammed Trump for signing an executive order Thursday that formally renamed Lake Ontario, which is shared between New York and Canada, to “Lake America.”

“We’re a deeply unserious country right now,” Sellers said during a CNN panel discussion. “I mean, the fact is, Lake Ontario, the name is over 400 years old. It predates the Confederation of Canada. It predates the Declaration of Independence. Like, what are we doing?”

The name change is the latest flash point between the two nations, which announced a series of tit-for-tat tariffs after Canada backed out of trade negotiations with the U.S.

Trump announced 50 percent tariffs on $20 billion worth of Canadian imports. Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney, in response, announced “dollar for dollar” retaliatory tariffs.

Carney slammed the Trump administration for the move to rename the lake, citing its existence well before Canada became a country and before the signing of the U.S. Declaration of Independence. Other Canadian officials also aired their disagreement over the name change, which Canada is not required to adhere to.

Trump has renamed other prominent landmarks during his second term. On the first day of his second term, he signed an executive order renaming the Gulf of Mexico to the “Gulf of America.”

articles.title: Hegseth ignored Centcom, cut program ahead of Iran school strike: Report
articles.summary: What kind of leader asks his top military commanders for advice and then ignores them because he doesn’t like the answer? Apparently Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth.
articles.body:
What kind of leader asks his top military commanders for advice and then ignores them because he doesn’t like the answer? Apparently Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth.

New reporting from ProPublica reveals that some of the nation’s top military commanders were polled by Hegseth about cutting a program called Civilian Harm Mitigation and Response, which was designed to reduce civilian casualties during U.S. military operations. The report notes that the top military officials overwhelmingly wanted to keep the program in place.

Central Command, which oversees U.S. military operations across much of the Middle East, specifically warned that scaling it back could increase the risk of misidentifying targets and reduce awareness on the battlefield.

The reporting shows Hegseth viewed civilian-harm mitigation as part of a culture that was too politically correct and incompatible with his vision of the Department of War.

The Civilian Harm Mitigation and Response program was designed to improve targeting, understand conditions on the ground and reduce mistakes. Central Command told Hegseth’s staff that the work enhanced precision and accuracy.

The consequences of Hegseth’s decision to dismantle that infrastructure are hard to ignore. Hegseth gutted the effort, stripping it of almost all of its funding, while the U.S. was actively launching new campaigns in Somalia, Yemen and Iran, according to the report.

You’ll remember early on in this war with Iran, a U.S. airstrike hit a school in Minab , a city near the Strait of Hormuz, killing more than 100 children and creating a firestorm of national and international outrage.

Hegseth was questioned about the strike before Congress and promised to investigate. No public reports of that investigation have been released, but it’s been reported that the Department of War blamed the incident on outdated U.S. intelligence.

Now members of Congress are asking whether the decision to gut civilian-protection capabilities played a role in the Iran school tragedy as well.

You may remember 11 senators sent a letter to Hegseth in April of this year, where they said, in part, that the school strike, as well as other deadly attacks on civilians in Iran, reflected “the administration’s broader disregard for the strategic, legal, and moral imperative to minimize civilian harm.” It went on to say, “This is a concerning pattern and raises questions about whether the administration is upholding international law and the laws of war.”

With this new reporting, we should all be asking that question, too. Real leadership isn’t about being the loudest person in the room. It’s about knowing when to listen to the people who have spent their careers understanding the consequences of getting something wrong — especially when the stakes are human lives.

Lindsey Granger is a NewsNation contributor and co-host of The Hill’s commentary show “Rising.” This column is an edited transcription of her on-air commentary.

President Trump will not be traveling to New York City for the 25th anniversary of the Sept. 11 terror attacks, according to The Hill’s sister network NewsNation.

A White House official told the network that Vice President Vance is “still traveling to NYC and all three sites will be represented with administration officials in attendance.”

The New York Times and CNN reported Friday that Trump will deliver remarks at the Pentagon to mark the anniversary.

According to the Times, Trump was interested in delivering remarks at the Ground Zero sight in Manhattan on the anniversary. However, since 2012, politicians have not been allowed to deliver remarks at the site.

The publication also noted that other factors played into the decision for Trump to mark the anniversary at the Pentagon, including his trip the next day to his golf course in Doonbeg, Ireland, which is hosting the Irish Open.

“As a proud New Yorker, President Trump has spoken about his own experiences watching the horrific events of September 11, 2001,” White House spokesperson Anna Kelly said in a statement when asked where Trump will mark the anniversary

“On the 25th anniversary of this tragic day, the President will remember those who were killed at the hands of evil terrorists, honor their loved ones, and pay tribute to the brave first responders who put their lives on the line to rescue their fellow Americans,” she continued.

This will be the second year in a row Trump has marked the anniversary at the Pentagon.

In 2024, Trump and Vance attended the ceremony at Ground Zero. Former President Biden and former Vice President Kamala Harris were also in attendance.

articles.summary: 💧Plus: Another ripple in US-Canada relations {beacon} It’s Friday. Leaf your worries behind — fall is almost here (or so my allergies believe). In today’s issue: Warsh takes on inflation U.S.-Canada trade war makes waves Six months later, Iran war grinds on Mail-in ballot rules hit the brakes Programming note: Hello! We are…
articles.body:
It’s Friday. Leaf your worries behind — fall is almost here (or so my allergies believe).

Programming note : Hello! We are Steff Danielle Thomas and Colin Meyn filling in for Cate. Please send your tips, comments and story ideas to sthomas@thehill.com or cmeyn@thehill.com .

The Associated Press | Mark Schiefelbein

Federal Reserve Chair Kevin Warsh used his closely watched speech Friday in Jackson Hole, Wyo., to send a pretty clear message : Inflation is still too high , and the Fed isn’t ruling out doing more about it.

Warsh said the central bank needs to see inflation moving “clearly and at sufficient speed” toward its 2 percent target — otherwise, “we have work to do.” He also said responsibility for controlling inflation “sits squarely” with the Fed.

Translation: Interest rate hikes could be on the horizon. While he did not commit to a move or timeline — keeping with his aversion to giving markets “forward guidance” — Warsh suggested current rates may not be doing much to slow the economy.

The Trump factor: President Trump has spent most of his second term pushing the Fed to lower borrowing costs — a pressure campaign that began under former Fed Chair Jerome Powell . The new chair’s Friday message cuts against that push.

The Fed panel in charge of rate decisions will meet Sept. 15-16. While rates may remain steady at that meeting, the chances of a hike this year appear to be rising.

📰 Read more here from The Hill’s Miranda Nazzaro .

Trump signed an executive order Thursday to change the name of Lake Ontario to “Lake America,” following through on an idea he floated earlier in the week as tensions with Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney escalated.

Canada says, not so fast : Carney responded with a little history lesson, noting that Lake Ontario’s name comes from the Wendat word Ontari’io and has been used for more than 400 years — longer than either Canada or the United States has existed as a country.

“We know that America is changing … Canadians also know that naming reality means calling it Lake Ontario — then, now and always,” he wrote online .

Meanwhile, Ottawa is preparing tariffs as high as 50 percent on $27.6 billion worth of U.S. imports beginning Sept. 8, matching Trump’s tariffs “dollar for dollar, rate for rate.”

The Trump administration isn’t exactly shrugging that off, either. U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer warned earlier this week that Washington won’t “just sit down and take” further retaliation from Canada.

Trump is trying to give Americans a break on ground beef prices — but farmers and ranchers are really angry about it. The plan to temporarily allow more imported beef at lower tariff rates is also a rare move from the president that has drawn almost unanimous pushback in his party.

On Friday, he turned his attention to meat processors, announcing plans to give farmers and ranchers more freedom to process and sell their own products.

But will it be enough to ease their frustration?

The hard-line Iranian regime that Trump hoped to overthrow is still firmly in place and showing no signs of folding on its nuclear program. But it’s not all bad news.

The U.S. Navy appears to have facilitated fairly steady traffic through the Strait of Hormuz.

How much? Last week’s ship traffic was up 50 percent from the week before, according to Lloyd’s List Intelligence. The Trump administration has said 9 million barrels are passing through the strait each day, while some analysts suggest the number is closer to 2 million to 6 million barrels each day. It was closer to 15 million barrels a day before the war.

Gas prices are holding steady around $4 a gallon, high enough to cause midterm headaches for Republicans but not as high as some had feared.

This Guardian story is worth a read : Trump’s war on Iran is rapidly draining US navy budget, documents and interviews reveal

So, what next? Iran and Oman are still negotiating a bilateral agreement on shared control of the Strait of Hormuz, which runs between the two countries.

The U.S. isn’t directly involved, but Iran wants America’s naval blockade lifted as part of any agreement. Mediators from Qatar and Pakistan are trying to get Washington and Tehran back to the table.

The president lashed out at Fox News correspondent Jonathan Hunt over a report that U.S. leaders are set to meet with Group of 20 leaders to increase pressure on Iran. Trump seemed to interpret the report as saying the U.S. was anxious to meet with Iran, writing, “I don’t want to meet, they do. In fact, they are begging to make a deal. Bret Baier should straighten out his flunkies, for a change!” Baier responded to the president before the show ended. “First of all, Jonathan is not a flunky. He is a great reporter,” the anchor said. “Second of all, Mr. President, we didn’t say you wanted to meet.”

The Trump administration’s new mail-in voting restrictions are on hold again after a dizzying week of legal back-and-forth.

What’s new: A federal judge in Boston late Thursday temporarily blocked a new U.S. Postal Service rule requiring mail ballots to meet specific design standards, including a unique logo and barcode with an embedded ZIP code. The order lasts 14 days — extending beyond when some states will begin sending absentee and overseas ballots.

Legal whiplash: The Supreme Court on Monday lifted an earlier block, ruling that states had sued too soon because the Postal Service hadn’t finalized its rule. When the rule hit the federal register on Wednesday, Democratic-led states essentially said “game on” and headed straight back to court . By Thursday night, the restrictions were paused again.

All of this legal ping-pong comes with the midterms just more than two months away. The ball is quickly heading back to the Supreme Court.

articles.body:
California Gov. Gavin Newsom (D) — a likely presidential candidate in 2028 — will head to the South next week on a four-day, three-state sweep covering 10 counties, as part of his “Take it Back Tour,” his office announced Friday.

As part of the tour, which begins Wednesday, Newsom will visit South Carolina, which the Democratic National Committee recently announced would vote first in the Democratic primary in January 2028. The tour also will take him to Alabama and North Carolina.

“Governor Newsom is returning to the places where these fights were first won — and where MAGA’s rollback of rights carries the most weight today,” a press release announcing the tour reads.

“The lesson of the south is that rights are never guaranteed — they have to be won, and then defended,” the release states.

In South Carolina, where Newsom is expected to spend two days traveling the state, he will focus on downballot races, traveling through Jasper, Beaufort, and Dorchester counties — three counties Trump won in the 2024 presidential race.

In North Carolina, Newsom will campaign in the Charlotte area, where he will canvass with local Democrats and fundraise for key races.

In Alabama, Newsom is expected to walk the U.S. Civil Rights Trail with local civil rights leaders.

Earlier this month, Newsom traveled to battleground Michigan , where he met with Abdul El-Sayed, the Democrat vying for the Senate. He also appeared at an event with autoworkers and local leaders to help get out the vote for Democrats competing in the state.

A federal judge on Friday rejected President Trump’s latest bid to fight his criminal conviction outside of New York’s state courts, a strategy aimed at citing presidential immunity , under which Trump could potentially toss charges that stem from a 2016 hush money payment in the trash can.

U.S. District Judge Alvin Hellerstein has denied Trump’s attempts to move to federal court three times . An appeals panel had directed Hellerstein to take another look, saying he brushed aside the president’s arguments too easily.

Hellerstein on Friday reaffirmed that Trump was too late and that the verdict withstands presidential immunity anyway.

“The grounds for a second removal cited by Defendant, Donald J. Trump, are neither new nor legally sufficient. He has failed to show good cause and diligence,” the judge wrote .

Hellerstein is an appointee of former President Clinton who serves on the federal bench in Manhattan.

Trump was convicted on 34 counts of falsifying business records in connection with a $130,000 hush money payment to adult film star Stormy Daniels to cover up an alleged affair.

Trump’s legal loss comes as prosecutors’ star witness, Michael Cohen, the president’s ex-fixer-turned-enemy who made the payment, has reconciled with his former boss . Cohen has recently said he was coerced to testify, leading Trump to claim he was “weaponized.”

The hush money case was one of four criminal prosecutions that Trump faced as he campaigned for another White House term. The New York case was the only one to go to trial; the others were dismissed.

Trump is still appealing his conviction in New York’s state courts, but he has hoped to instead advance his arguments before a federal judge.

Congress allows federal officials to move courts when they are being prosecuted for matters related to “any act under color” of their office. The arrangement is aimed at preventing state interference, ensuring the official can have a neutral forum.

Trump launched an original attempt to move courts before his trial. Hellerstein rejected the bid.

After Manhattan District Attorney Alvin Bragg’s (D) office secured the conviction, Trump made another ask. This time, he had the Supreme Court’s landmark decision that former presidents are entitled to broad criminal immunity in his pocket. Trump argued it meant his New York conviction could no longer stand .

“They do not; paying hush money to an adult film star or engaging in a cover-up of an embarrassment are not subsumed in presidential immunity,” Hellerstein pushed back in his ruling.

Every judge to consider the argument directly so far has rejected it.

In November, the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 2nd Circuit ruled that Hellerstein bypassed important issues and needed to reconsider Trump’s ask to move to federal courts so he could advance the argument.

A spokesperson for the Manhattan district attorney’s office declined to comment.

“The Supreme Court’s historic decision on Immunity, the Federal and New York State Constitutions, and other established legal precedent mandate that the Witch Hunt perpetrated by the Manhattan DA be removed to federal court, and immediately overturned and dismissed,” a spokesperson for the president’s legal team said.

“President Trump has already prevailed in this case at the Second Circuit Court of Appeals, and today’s baseless and lawless decision contradicts that correct ruling. President Trump will be filing a powerful appeal, and will continue defeating Democrat weaponization at every turn.”

articles.body:
Civil rights leader the Rev. Al Sharpton, one of the organizers of this year’s March on Washington , compared New York Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (D) to the late congresswoman and presidential candidate Shirley Chisholm (D-N.Y.) while introducing her at the event.

“I know people, I was Shirley Chisolm’s youth director,” Sharpton stated on stage while introducing Ocasio-Cortez, before declaring Chisolm “had the same fire and vigor as this beloved sister of mine,” referring to Ocasio-Cortez.

During his introduction, Sharpton also called Ocasio-Cortez “a sister beloved who has stood up on these issues and spoke out on what needed to be said.”

The comparison is notable as speculation mounts about Ocasio-Cortez potentially launching a presidential campaign of her own in 2028, with many seeing her as a potential standard-bearer for the Democratic Party’s left flank in the upcoming primary.

Chisolm, who like Ocasio-Cortez represented New York City in Congress, became the first Black woman to be elected to Congress in 1968. She became the first Black candidate to seek a major party’s presidential nomination and the first woman to seek the Democratic nomination.

Ocasio-Cortez spoke immediately following Vermont Sen. Bernie Sanders (I), the progressive juggernaut. He fell short of earning the presidential nomination in both the 2016 and 2020 Democratic primaries.

The speculation around the New York congresswoman comes as democratic socialists and progressives have notched several key victories this primary season and her name appears near the top of or leading most polls of Democratic presidential hopefuls.
